title: SHE WAS PREGNANT WITH HIS CHILD… BUT THE WOMAN WHO OWNED HER BEGAN TO HATE HER.
paragraphs: SHE WAS PREGNANT WITH HIS CHILD… BUT THE WOMAN WHO OWNED HER BEGAN TO HATE HER.
One pregnancy. One wounded marriage. One enslaved woman caught in the middle. And a God who saw what everyone else refused to see.
“And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.” — Genesis 16:4 (KJV)
Imagine discovering that you are pregnant… and instead of celebrating, you begin to fear what will happen when you walk into the next room.
The father of your child is the man of the house.
His wife is the woman who has authority over your life.
And the very people who placed you in this situation are now turning against you.
Where do you go when the people who made the decision are blaming you for its consequences?
Where do you run when the house you sleep in has become the place where your heart is being crushed?
And what happens when the people who speak about God's promises are the same people causing your pain?
This is not a modern family scandal.
This happened thousands of years ago.
Inside the household of Abram and Sarai.
And before this story ends, a pregnant Egyptian servant will discover something about God that many wounded people desperately need to hear today.
The God who makes promises to the powerful also sees the tears of the powerless.
But to understand how extraordinary that truth is, we have to enter a household where faith, desperation, jealousy, and human failure have become dangerously entangled.
God had promised Abram descendants.
Not a handful.
A multitude.
Genesis 15:5 records God's invitation for Abram to look toward heaven and count the stars, if he could count them. So would his offspring be.
It was a magnificent promise.
But there was a painful reality.
Sarai had no child.
Year after year, the promise remained.
And year after year, the cradle remained empty.
If you have ever prayed for something that seemed to come easily to everyone else, perhaps you understand a small part of that ache.
You celebrate another person's blessing while privately wondering when your own season will come.
You smile.
You congratulate.
You say God is faithful.
And then you return to a quiet room where the question you are afraid to speak waits for you.
Lord, have You forgotten me?
Scripture does not tell us every private thought Sarai experienced. We must be careful not to pretend that it does.
But it does tell us that she was unable to bear children, and that her household eventually attempted to resolve that painful situation through a human arrangement.
Genesis 16:2 records Sarai telling Abram to go in to Hagar, her Egyptian servant, in the hope that she might obtain children through her.
That arrangement existed within the ancient world's social structures, where enslaved women could be used for their owners' reproductive purposes.
But the fact that something was practiced in an ancient society does not mean God approved of every part of it.
And here is a truth we cannot afford to miss.
A practice can be culturally accepted and still leave human beings deeply wounded.
Hagar was not introduced as an independent woman freely negotiating her future.
She was an Egyptian servant under Sarai's authority.
The text does not record her consent to this arrangement.
That silence matters.

Because too often, when we read Genesis 16, we talk about Abram's faith, Sarai's impatience, and the birth of Ishmael while barely noticing the woman whose body became the place where their decision unfolded.
Her name was Hagar.
She was not merely a plot device in someone else's spiritual journey.
She was a human being.
And God knew her name.
Then came the pregnancy.
Genesis 16:4 tells us that Abram went in to Hagar, she conceived, and afterward Sarai became despised in Hagar's eyes.
The Hebrew expression is especially revealing.
וַתֵּקַל גְּבִרְתָּהּ בְּעֵינֶיהָ
Vattēqal gevirtāh be‘ênêhā.
Literally, the sense is that her mistress became light, or diminished, in her eyes.
The Hebrew verb is related to קָלַל (qalal), which can carry the idea of being light, insignificant, or treated with contempt.
This is why translations speak of Sarai being despised or looked upon with contempt.
It describes a deterioration in Hagar's regard for Sarai.
But notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not disclose every thought in Hagar's mind.
It does not explain all the emotions behind her changed attitude.
It does not authorize us to invent conversations or motives that Scripture never records.
Perhaps her pregnancy altered how she viewed her position. Perhaps the household's power dynamics intensified existing tensions.
We can recognize those possibilities without presenting them as established facts.
What we know is enough.
The relationship became bitter.
And bitterness rarely remains confined to the heart.
Sarai saw what was happening.
And she was angry.
Genesis 16:5 records her complaint to Abram:
“My wrong be upon thee.”
She had proposed the arrangement.
Abram had agreed.
Hagar had conceived.
Now Sarai held Abram responsible for the humiliation she experienced.
And suddenly the promise they had been waiting for had become entangled with resentment.
Have you ever watched something you thought would solve a problem create a deeper one?
A decision made because you were tired of waiting.
A relationship entered because you were afraid of being alone.
A compromise justified because the outcome looked promising.
A door forced open because heaven seemed silent.
Then the consequences arrived.
And you discovered that getting what you wanted was not the same as receiving peace.
There is a warning here, but it must be handled carefully.
The problem was not that Sarai longed for a child. The problem was the human harm bound up in the way the household pursued that longing.
Desire is not automatically sin.
Waiting is not automatically unbelief.
And suffering is not proof that someone has failed God.
But desperation can tempt us to treat people as instruments for reaching our desired future.
That is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because we may never have stood inside Abram's household.
But many of us know what it means to be caught inside someone else's decisions.
A parent makes a choice, and the child carries the wound.
A leader protects a reputation, and the vulnerable person bears the consequences.
A spouse refuses accountability, and the family absorbs the damage.
Someone with power creates a crisis, then demands that someone with less power quietly endure it.
Hagar's story forces us to ask a question we might prefer to avoid.
When our plans hurt another person, are we willing to recognize their suffering, or do we become angry when they no longer see us the same way?
Then Abram spoke.
Genesis 16:6 records his response to Sarai:
“Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee.”
Read that again.
He was the father of the child Hagar carried.
He was the man whose household had brought her into this situation.
And when the conflict became unbearable, he placed her back under Sarai's authority.
There is no recorded defense of Hagar in his response.
No recorded intervention to protect her from what followed.
Instead, the text says Sarai dealt harshly with her.
The Hebrew is:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי
Vatte‘annehā Saray.
The verb comes from עָנָה (‘anah), which in this context means to afflict, oppress, or treat harshly.
It is not a mild description of an uncomfortable disagreement.
The same Hebrew root is used elsewhere for serious affliction, including Israel's oppression in Egypt in Exodus 1:11–12.
Genesis does not describe every act Sarai committed against Hagar, so we should not invent specific forms of abuse.
But the biblical description is unmistakably serious.
Hagar was afflicted.
And she fled.
A pregnant woman.
An Egyptian servant.
Leaving a household with resources and protection, heading into the uncertainty of the wilderness.
We do not know every fear that accompanied her departure.
But we know she was running from harsh treatment.
And this is where the story changes.
Because the people who should have protected her had failed her.
But God had not lost sight of her.
Genesis 16:7 says:
“And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness.”
Found her.
What a remarkable phrase.
Hagar was fleeing.
Yet the biblical narrative does not portray her as invisible.
The messenger of the LORD encountered her beside a spring on the road to Shur.
And then came a question.
“Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?” — Genesis 16:8 (KJV)
God's messenger addressed her by name.
Hagar.
Not merely by her usefulness.
Not merely by her pregnancy.
Not merely as the woman at the center of Abram and Sarai's conflict.
Hagar.
Her answer was painfully direct.
“I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
No elaborate explanation.
No carefully polished testimony.
Just the truth.
She was running.
There are moments when spiritual honesty begins with words that simple.
I am hurting.
I am afraid.
I do not know what to do.
I cannot pretend anymore.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to sound stronger than you feel.
You tell people you are fine because explaining your pain is exhausting.
You serve in church while carrying grief nobody notices.
You encourage others while privately wondering whether anyone would recognize your own exhaustion.
You believe God sees everything.
But sometimes you still wonder whether He sees you.
Hagar's encounter speaks directly into that question.
Yet we must not rush past the difficult part.
The messenger instructed Hagar to return to Sarai and submit to her authority.
That command belongs to this specific biblical encounter. It must never be turned into a blanket instruction that abused people should return to dangerous situations or remain under oppression.
Scripture records a particular divine direction to Hagar; it does not give modern abusers permission to demand submission or silence.
If you are experiencing abuse, seeking safety, protection, and trustworthy help is not a betrayal of faith.
And we should remember that Genesis does not describe Hagar's suffering as good.
God's attention to her does not excuse the people who harmed her.
The encounter also contained a promise.
Genesis 16:10 records the messenger declaring that Hagar's descendants would be multiplied beyond counting.
Then came the announcement of her son's name.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma‘el.
Ishmael.
A name connected to the Hebrew words for hearing and God.
The explanation is given in Genesis 16:11:
“Because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.”
The Hebrew name communicates the truth:
God hears.
Not because Hagar had escaped every consequence.
Not because her circumstances had suddenly become easy.
Not because every relationship in her life had been restored.
But because her suffering had not escaped divine attention.
And then Hagar spoke words that would echo across generations.
Genesis 16:13 says:
“Thou God seest me.”
The Hebrew expression is:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro’i.
Often understood as “You are a God who sees me.”
The passage's Hebrew wording and the surrounding explanation have interpretive complexities, but its central testimony is clear: Hagar recognized the extraordinary reality of being seen by God.
Think about the contrast.
In Abram's household, she was identified by her position.
In the wilderness, she was addressed by her name.
In the household, her pregnancy intensified conflict.
In the wilderness, her unborn child received a name carrying the testimony that God had heard her affliction.
The woman who fled human cruelty encountered divine attention.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has needed for years.
Being overlooked by people does not mean you have been overlooked by God.
But Hagar's story does not end in Genesis 16.
Years later, another crisis would come.
Genesis 21 records Hagar and Ishmael being sent away after Isaac's birth.
This time, their water ran out in the wilderness.
Hagar placed her child under a shrub and moved away because she could not bear to watch him die.
The text records her weeping.
And then Genesis 21:17 says:
“And God heard the voice of the lad.”
There it is again.
God heard.
The name Ishmael was not an empty religious slogan.
The God who had heard Hagar's affliction had not become deaf to the cries of her son.
God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of water.
The narrative does not say that God magically erased every hardship in her future.
But it shows that He had not abandoned them in that moment of desperate need.
And now we must ask the question that brings this ancient story into the center of the Gospel.
What does Hagar's story reveal about Jesus Christ?
We should not pretend that Genesis 16 explicitly names Jesus or that every detail of Hagar's experience is a hidden prediction of the cross.
It does not.
But when we read Scripture as a whole, we encounter the same divine character revealed with breathtaking fullness in Jesus Christ.
The God who saw an afflicted servant in the wilderness is the God whose Son entered a world of suffering.
Jesus did not build His ministry around flattering the powerful.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the rejected.
He spoke with people whose reputations made others uncomfortable.
He noticed those who were easily ignored.
In Luke 7:13, when Jesus encountered a widow grieving her only son, Scripture says He had compassion on her.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman at a well and revealed knowledge of her life without treating her as disposable.
In Luke 19:10, Jesus declared that the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
And at the cross, the sinless Savior bore the sins of others.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
This is where the Gospel goes beyond the comfort of knowing that God sees our pain.
Jesus came not only to comfort sinners in their brokenness, but to rescue them from sin and reconcile them to God.
Because if we read Hagar's story carefully, we cannot divide humanity into a simple world of innocent sufferers and wicked offenders.
We encounter real oppression.
We encounter resentment.
We encounter failures of responsibility.
We encounter wounded people whose responses may also be complicated.
And if we are honest, we may recognize ourselves in more than one place.
Sometimes we have been Hagar, wounded by decisions we never controlled.
Sometimes we have acted like Sarai, allowing frustration to turn into harshness toward another person.
Sometimes we have acted like Abram, avoiding responsibility when intervention would have required courage.
That recognition should not erase the profound differences in power and responsibility between these individuals.
It should lead us to examine our own hearts without blaming the oppressed for their oppression.
Because the Gospel is not merely an invitation to identify the wrongs committed against us.
It is also a summons to acknowledge the sins within us.
Have we used our influence to protect ourselves at another person's expense?
Have we allowed jealousy to become cruelty?
Have we watched someone suffer and chosen silence because speaking would be inconvenient?
Have we mistaken religious activity for genuine obedience?
Have we asked God to bless our plans while ignoring the people those plans might harm?
These are not comfortable questions.
But conviction can become a doorway to repentance.
And repentance, through Jesus Christ, is not the end of hope.
It is the beginning of returning to the One who gives grace.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)
Notice what this promise does not say.
It does not say we are forgiven because we have suffered enough.
It does not say our good works can purchase mercy.
It does not say we can undo every consequence of our actions through religious effort.
Forgiveness rests on the faithfulness and justice of God, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And genuine repentance bears fruit in changed lives.
If we have wounded someone, repentance may require confession, accountability, restitution where possible, and a willingness to stop repeating the harm.
If we have been wounded, grace does not require us to deny what happened.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending abuse was acceptable.
Reconciliation, where possible, requires truth and cannot be demanded at the expense of someone's safety.
Jesus does not redeem people by teaching them to call evil good.
He brings us into the light.
And the light exposes what darkness has tried to hide.
Maybe that is why Hagar's story still unsettles us.
Because it reminds us that a household can speak about God's promises while still treating someone unjustly.
A person can know the language of faith and still need to repent.
A family can carry a sacred calling and still experience devastating dysfunction.
But human failure does not make God's character unfaithful.
Abram and Sarai's story would continue.
God would fulfill His promise concerning Isaac.
Hagar and Ishmael would not disappear from His concern.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ would come as the promised offspring through whom God's blessing reaches the nations, as the New Testament explains in Galatians 3:16.
That is the larger story.
Not that every painful decision becomes righteous because God can work beyond it.
Not that every wounded relationship will be repaired exactly as we hope.
Not that believers will be spared wilderness seasons.
But that God remains faithful to His purposes, even when human beings act with weakness, fear, and sin.
And in Jesus Christ, the invitation to receive mercy reaches people who have nothing to boast about.
The wounded can come.
The ashamed can come.
The repentant sinner can come.
The exhausted believer can come.
The person who has spent years hiding behind a respectable appearance can come.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Not because every burden is imaginary.
Not because every wound disappears overnight.
But because the Savior is worthy of our trust.
And perhaps today, the most courageous prayer you can offer is not a beautiful prayer.
Perhaps it is simply:
Lord Jesus, You see what happened.
You see what I have done.
You see what I have carried.
You know the bitterness I have allowed to grow.
You know the wounds I have hidden.
Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken in me. Give me courage to obey Your truth. Teach me to trust You without harming others or surrendering to despair.
I cannot rewrite yesterday.
But I believe You can redeem a life surrendered to You.
Amen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be living through a season that feels painfully similar to Hagar's wilderness.
They may be carrying a burden nobody knows about.
They may be questioning whether God notices their suffering.
They may be surrounded by religious words but starving for genuine compassion.
Not because an algorithm determines the value of a soul.
But because Scripture has a way of reaching people at moments when human encouragement is not enough.
I also want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to publish the details of your wounds to be worthy of prayer.
There may be someone reading your words who recognizes their own struggle and realizes they are not alone.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish articles.
Not merely to gather reactions.
But to keep bringing people back to the Scriptures, to the person of Jesus Christ, and to the transforming truth of the Gospel.
We want this to be a place where people can encounter biblical truth, thoughtful encouragement, conviction that leads to repentance, and hope rooted in Christ rather than empty promises.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and expand, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Scripture teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
And that same verse teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
So this invitation is not a demand.
You cannot purchase God's favor through a monthly payment.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
These products are not the reason to support the Gospel.
They are simply one way we hope to express appreciation to those who help make the ministry's work possible.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their walk with Jesus, and continue learning beyond a single article.
Jesus Christ must remain the center.
Not a platform.
Not merchandise.
Not the person writing the article.
Jesus.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms lives through His grace.
And as you leave this story, remember Hagar.
Remember the bitterness inside that household.
Remember the failures of those who held power.
Remember the pregnant woman fleeing into the wilderness.
Remember the spring.
Remember the question.
Remember the name.
Hagar.
And remember the testimony she carried from that encounter.
You are a God who sees me.
The wilderness did not erase her identity.
The cruelty she experienced did not make her invisible to God.
And the failures of human beings did not cancel His compassion.
Now carry that truth into your own life.
If you have sinned, turn to Jesus in repentance.
If you have been wounded, bring your pain before Him and seek the help and protection you need.
If you have power over others, use it with humility and justice.
If you have been silent while someone suffered, ask God for courage to act rightly.
And if you have spent years believing that your life is too damaged to matter, remember that the Gospel is not the announcement that good people have earned a second chance.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The cross reveals the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of our Savior.
And grace calls us not merely to feel better about yesterday, but to become new in Christ.
The people who wounded Hagar may have treated her as though she were invisible, but the God who found her in the wilderness knew her name before she ever cried out to Him.
